issues.explanation: Occupation 'Retired' is implausible for age 28 (retired is implausible if age < 50).

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits awkwardly with 'my memories are very clear and detailed' and 'mostly pictures or images' for a PTSD profile tied to a life-threatening accident; this pattern suggests unusually easy verbal processing despite vivid intrusive-style memory, which weakens coherence of the memory node.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking whether someone is following him implies an interpersonal pursuit/assault-type danger theme, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being a life-threatening accident and with the rest of the profile, which does not otherwise indicate persecution-related threat.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' also implies an interpersonal harm/blame theme that does not fit well with the accident trauma context or the other selected appraisals, memories, and threats.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other items describe accident-related sensory threat (loud sounds, startle), image-based trauma memory, and self-critical appraisals, with maladaptive responses centered on avoidance/removal from reminders and rumination/meaning seeking. Undereating introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, making it the least clinically coherent item in this five-component profile.

vignette:
Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was fifty-two when a construction crane collapsed on the set of his latest film. He had been standing near the edge of the soundstage, reviewing footage on a monitor, when a sudden metallic shriek cut through the ambient noise—a sound he would later describe as the world tearing open. The crane's arm fell in slow motion and then all at once, crushing the lighting rig beside him. He felt the percussion of impact through his chest, saw the shower of sparks, tasted metal and dust. For three seconds he could not move. Then his assistant was pulling him backward, and he was on the ground, gasping, certain he was dying. The hospital confirmed what the emergency room doctor told him: he had escaped by less than a meter. A fracture in his left radius, lacerations, but alive. The crane operator had suffered a catastrophic mechanical failure—nothing Marcus could have foreseen or prevented. And yet, for the past eighteen months, that distinction had become increasingly difficult to hold.

The nightmares began within a week. Marcus would wake at two or three in the morning with his heart hammering, the image of the falling crane suspended in perfect, merciless clarity behind his eyes. The memory had a photographic quality that unnerved him—not a narrative he could tell but a series of stills: the monitor screen, the shadow crossing the floor, the arc of metal against the grid lights. When he tried to describe it to his partner, David, the words felt inadequate, almost absurd. How could he explain the way the memory didn't feel like something that had happened but something that was still happening, replayed in his nervous system every time a door slammed or a truck rumbled past their Brooklyn brownstone?

Within weeks, Marcus had begun to avoid the soundstage entirely. He told the studio he needed time to recover, that he would direct remotely. The lie felt safer than the truth: that stepping back into that space—even in daylight, even with the crane removed—triggered a cascade of panic that left him shaking for hours afterward. He filled his days with smaller distractions. He rewatched old films, scrolled through social media, organized his archive of photographs from past productions. Anything to keep his mind occupied, to prevent it from drifting back to those three seconds. The distraction worked, but only in the moment. Each time he looked away, the weight of what he was avoiding seemed to grow heavier.

What troubled Marcus most deeply was the person he had become. He had always prided himself on his composure under pressure, his ability to make split-second decisions with confidence. Now he found himself jumping at the sound of a dropped plate, his entire body flooding with adrenaline at a car horn outside the window. He was hypervigilant in ways he couldn't control—constantly scanning for threat, listening for the next unexpected sound that might herald disaster. The vividness of his memories, their intrusive visual clarity, convinced him that his reactions were evidence of fundamental weakness. A stronger person would have moved past this by now. A competent director, a capable man, would not be undone by a sound. This belief—that his persistent fear and startle response revealed him to be a lousy coper, fundamentally inadequate—drove him deeper into avoidance. He stopped attending industry events, declined social invitations, worked only on projects he could manage from home. Each time he avoided a situation, he told himself it was temporary, a necessary reprieve. But the reprieve never came. Instead, the avoidance seemed to amplify his sense of threat. The world outside his apartment felt increasingly dangerous, unpredictable. Sounds that most people would barely register—the beep of a delivery truck, the crash of construction work several blocks away—sent him into a state of acute vigilance, his body braced for impact.

The hyperalertness fed back into his memory in ways Marcus was only beginning to recognize. When he heard a loud noise, the vividness of his traumatic memory spiked, as if the sound had opened a door directly into that moment on the soundstage. His threat detection system, now permanently sensitized, interpreted the memory's clarity as confirmation that danger was imminent and inescapable. This cycle of threat and memory began to feel like proof of his inadequacy, evidence that he was broken in some irreparable way. By the time he contacted his therapist, Marcus had withdrawn from most of his life. David had grown quiet and distant, hurt by the rejection that Marcus's avoidance had created. Work had become a phantom thing—projects he managed through email, his creative voice reduced to typed comments on scripts he could barely focus on. He had come to believe that the man he used to be—decisive, engaged, unafraid—was gone, replaced by someone he no longer recognized. What he wanted most was to feel safe in his own body again. What he feared most was that the person he had been before the crane fell would never come back.
